definition: Local energy-based shape histogram (LESH) is a proposed image descriptor in computer vision.
details: It can be used to get a description of the underlying shape. The LESH feature descriptor is built on local energy model of feature perception, see e.g. phase congruency for more details. It encodes the underlying shape by accumulating local energy of the underlying signal along several filter orientations, several local histograms from different parts of the image/patch are generated and concatenated together into a 128-dimensional compact spatial histogram. It is designed to be scale invariant. The LESH features can be used in applications like shape-based image retrieval, medical image processing, object detection, and pose estimation.

explainer.lead: LESH is an image descriptor that characterises underlying shape by accumulating local energy across filter orientations. It matters as a compact, scale-invariant way to represent shape in computer vision.

tiers.eli5: It describes an object's outline by measuring how strongly its edges respond in several directions, then counting those responses in different patches.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it as a feature for shape-based image matching; a pitfall is that local histograms can lose fine spatial detail when concatenated into one vector.
tiers.paperLevel: Built on the local energy model of feature perception (see phase congruency), it accumulates local energy along several filter orientations and concatenates local histograms into a 128-dimensional compact spatial histogram, designed to be scale invariant.

explainer.example: A patch of an image is filtered at multiple orientations, local energy is accumulated, and histograms from different parts are concatenated into a 128-dimensional vector.
